errors.problem: karui / karai differ in one vowel, are both 3 morae, both hiatus, and sit 10 apart with no mention — while kirai/karai (a structurally identical one-vowel contrast) is assigned >=25. tsumetai / tsumaranai share the /tsum-/ onset and sit 6 apart with no mention.
errors.fix: Add both to the interference table. karai should move past #70 (it is in the free-placement tail by the list's own argument); tsumaranai's Block D position is fixed by dependency, so tsumetai should move earlier or karui later.

errors.problem: Two problems. (1) Register: yukai, saiwai, aimai and juudai are formal/written-register items — saiwai as a predicate and juudai are essentially news and print register, aimai is written/analytic — and the note itself concedes they sit at ledger positions 1500-4000. Padding the trap list with items the learner will not hear undermines the claim that enumeration makes the ear-rule reliable. (2) Omission: the note defines Tier A as hiatus -ai only, but tokui [0] (na-class, hiatus -ui, high conversational frequency: "eego ga tokui", "tokui na ryoori") is a genuine Tier-A trap under note 4's own -ai/-ii/-ui/-oi formulation and is absent. Under Tier B's definition, heeki [0] and daisuki [1] are also missing.
errors.fix: Add tokui to Tier A. Demote yukai, saiwai, aimai and juudai to a clearly-labelled "will arrive much later" annex so the working trap deck contains only kirai, shinpai, tokui, yakkai. Add heeki and daisuki to Tier B.

errors.item: note 16 — "12 shape-balanced i-adjectives arrive by roughly card #22"
errors.problem: False by the note's own criterion. Note 1 defines shape balance as 3 exemplars in each of the four shapes. By card #22 the -oi shape has only two members (sugoi #2, omoshiroi #9); the third, tsuyoi, does not arrive until #27. The 12-item shape-balanced threshold is met at #27, not #22, inside week 8 rather than week 7. The note's headline conclusion (na-adjectives bind, not i-adjectives) survives — the 8th na-adjective lands at #38 — but the margin claimed as "not close" is overstated by five cards.
errors.fix: Correct to #27. The claim is still directionally right; state the actual figures (i-minimum satisfied at #27, na-minimum at #38).

errors.item: Block D interference — "karui (#49) vs omoi (#34) ... 2-mora vs 3-mora"
errors.problem: karui is ka-ru-i, 3 morae. omoi is o-mo-i, 3 morae. Both are 3 morae, both are [0], both are hiatus-final. The stated mora contrast does not exist, and the "risk here is low" conclusion that follows from it is unsupported — by note 8's own three-strike heuristic this pair shares accent AND mora count AND (hiatus) final shape and should be separated further than 15, not less.
errors.fix: Correct the mora counts and re-rule the pair. Given the -ui/-oi shapes differ segmentally, a gap of 15 is probably still defensible, but the stated reasoning must be replaced.

errors.item: note 9(f) — "'he is old' is toshiue / toshiyori, not *furui hito"
errors.problem: toshiue means "older THAN someone" — it is inherently comparative and relational ("ani wa toshiue desu"), not a predicate meaning "old". toshiyori is a noun meaning "elderly person", not a property predicate. Neither renders "he is old". The natural expressions are "toshi o totteiru" or "nenpai da".
errors.fix: Replace with toshi o totteiru / nenpai. Keep the furui restriction, which is correct.

errors.problem: yokunai [2] and yokute [2] are both likely wrong. Japanese adjective negatives accent the mora before nai (takai [2] > takakunai [4]), which gives yokunai [3], not [2]. The -kute form of an accented adjective retains the accent one mora earlier (takakute [2]), which gives yokute [1], not [2]. Both are marked approximate, but they are shipped in a note whose entire purpose is a dedicated micro-paradigm deck, so they will be recorded as-is.
errors.fix: Verify against NHK before recording; expected values are yoku [1], yokatta [2], yokunai [3], yokute [1].

errors.item: note 7 — "it is the ONLY suppletive adjective in the language"
errors.problem: Terminologically wrong and it weakens the argument it is making. ii is not suppletive in the go/went sense: yoi is a coexisting full lexeme of the same word that inflects perfectly regularly (yoi, yoku, yokatta, yokunai, yokute). What ii has is a defective citation form restricted to the non-past attributive/predicative slot, with all other slots supplied by its regular variant. That is stem alternation plus defectiveness, not suppletion.
errors.fix: Restate as "ii is defective: it fills only the non-past slot, and every other slot is supplied by its regular variant yoi." The pedagogical treatment (quarantine, micro-deck, compound family) is correct and unaffected.

errors.problem: Every internal note reference is off. Item 7 and item 48 and Block A's interference say "see note 12" for the atsui verification, which is note 10. (2) "This also avoids five near-identical [2]-accented -oi/-ai cards" is factually wrong about the accents: akai [0], kiiroi [0], aoi [2], kuroi [2], shiroi [2] — they are not uniformly [2], and note 14 lists them correctly, contradicting note 13.

errors.problem: Adverbial taihen is formal/written register (taihen mooshiwake gozaimasen, taihen osewa ni narimashita). In casual conversation the intensifier slot is filled by totemo, sugoku/sugoi, meccha, chou. Flagging taihen as a conversational intensifier in a deck ranked against conversational corpora is a register error. Related, item 2's note that sugoi "feeds the intensifier sugoku" understates that the casual spoken intensifier is overwhelmingly bare sugoi (sugoi oishii) rather than sugoku.
errors.fix: Gloss taihen as "tough / awful" plus a register-marked note that the adverbial use is formal. Add bare sugoi as the casual intensifier form on card 2.

errors.problem: tsumaru is not a phantom. 詰まru is a real and reasonably frequent verb (hana ga tsumaru, nodo ga tsumaru, yotei ga tsumatteru), and tsumaranai is homophonous with its negative. The risk is therefore genuine ambiguity with a real lexeme, not a back-formation to something nonexistent — which changes the card design: the learner needs the two senses disambiguated, not merely warned off an invented form. abunai and kitanai, by contrast, do have no positive.
errors.fix: Restate the risk for tsumaranai as collision with the real verb tsumaru, and keep the pure lexical-exception framing for abunai and kitanai.

errors.problem: dame does not mean broken. It means no good / not allowed / won't do. "Kono terebi wa dame da" can implicate a fault, but that is inference from context, not sense; the word for broken is kowareteru.
errors.fix: Drop "broken" from the gloss.

Since the brief's whole demand is an enumerated ledger, an item acknowledged as necessary must appear in it with a number.
verdict: Reject pending major revision. This is a serious piece of work — the block structure, the induction-gate framing, the atsui accent split, the kirai/kiree romanization argument, and the decision to defer the lexical -nai class are all genuinely well reasoned, and the accent integers are correct in roughly 55 of 63 cases. But it fails on its own terms in six places. Three are structural: (1) yasui is misclassified as -ai in three separate tables, which collapses the "-ui ends at exactly 4, the binding constraint" narrative that Block C's entire membership is justified by — the real count is 5 and nothing binds; (2) note 4's "hard diagnostic," the payoff the whole exception enumeration is built to deliver, is false as stated, because hiatus -ai/-oi/-ui is the ending of hundreds of common nouns, a fact note 11 concedes about omoi two notes later; (3) note 5's "-ee cannot be an i-adjective" contradicts the plan's own contraction-citation contract, under which takee, sugee, yabee and abunee are exactly what the learner hears. Two more are the specific failure this review exists to catch — a principle stated and then not applied: note 8's three-strike separation heuristic is violated twice in Block E alone (amai/akai at 2 apart, wakai/yowai adjacent, both identical on accent, mora count and final shape), and the stated ±10 shuffle budget cannot generate separations of 25-42 that the same document declares mandatory. The sixth is the omission of nai, which is not a tail item but arguably the most frequent adjective in the language and the anchor the #41-44 block is defined against. Six further high-frequency items (yabai, mottainai, onaji, daisuki, hazukashii, tokui) are missing outright, and the Tier-A trap list is padded with four written-register items (yukai, saiwai, aimai, juudai) while omitting the one conversationally frequent trap that breaks the diagnostic. Every internal note cross-reference is also misnumbered. Fix the yasui shape error and re-derive the gate arithmetic first — several downstream rationales change once it is corrected.
